segments.t: The meeting is over, and the agents spill back out into the corridors. In there, Gabriel finally admitted that Tarantino won't cast Cécile because they find her too old, and Samuel had to stop Mathias from blaming him for losing a deal worth millions. Now we follow Magali, Andréa's assistant. She has worked day and night for Andréa, she's exhausted, and today her mind is made up. First the whole scene in French; don't try to catch everything, the gist is enough.
Magali! Tu as une enveloppe?
J'en ai assez. Je pars!
Tu vas où?
Ne fais pas ça, Magali.
Je n'en peux plus, Andréa.
Je suis très fatiguée.
Bien sûr que tu es fatiguée.
On est tous fatigués. C'est l'hiver!
Prends de la gelée royale.
Fais du vélo! Ça donne des forces.
C'est comme ça que tu me remercies?
C'est moi qui t'ai formée!
Je ne veux pas l'entendre!
Je veux juste partir.
Tu ne pars pas. C'est moi qui te vire!
Tu es virée!
Let's take it slowly. Andréa is on the phone as usual, and she shouts across the office for something small.
Magali! Tu as une enveloppe?
'Magali! Have you got an envelope?' Andréa uses the casual 'you' with her assistant, as everyone does at the agency. But Magali isn't fetching envelopes today.
J'en ai assez. Je pars!
'I've had enough. I'm leaving!' The first sentence is a fixed expression for being fed up, worth learning as one block. Andréa doesn't take it seriously at first.
Tu vas où?
'Where are you going?' In everyday speech the question word can come at the very end, after the verb. Then Andréa gives an order.
Ne fais pas ça, Magali.

'Don't do this, Magali.' Here's our first grammar point: commands. With the casual 'you', you simply drop the pronoun and use the verb on its own. To make it negative, you wrap it in the two little words of 'not'. Magali answers.
Je n'en peux plus, Andréa.
'I can't take any more, Andréa.' Literally 'I can no more of it'. People say it when they're at the end of their rope. And she says it plainly.
Je suis très fatiguée.
'I'm very tired.' Second grammar point: listen to the last word. Written down, it gets an extra letter because Magali is a woman, but it sounds exactly the same. Andréa has an answer for everything.
Bien sûr que tu es fatiguée.
'Of course you're tired.' The same word for tired, and again in its feminine spelling. Then Andréa shrugs.
On est tous fatigués. C'est l'hiver!
'We're all tired. It's winter!' This time the word for tired is plural, because it's about everybody. The little word at the start means 'we' in casual French. Now come her famous tips.
Prends de la gelée royale.
'Take some royal jelly.' Another command, built from the verb 'to take'. Royal jelly is a health food made by bees, which is a funny cure for a burned-out assistant. Andréa has another idea.
Fais du vélo! Ça donne des forces.

'Ride a bike! It gives you energy.' One more casual command, from the verb 'to do'. Magali's answer is not polite at all: she says that if she stays, she might end up hitting Andréa. So Andréa plays the victim.
C'est comme ça que tu me remercies?
'Is this how you thank me?' Literally 'it's like that that you thank me?'. A typical way to sound hurt. And she reminds Magali of everything she did for her.
C'est moi qui t'ai formée!
'I'm the one who trained you!' The pattern 'it's me who' puts the spotlight on Andréa. The verb ends with that extra feminine letter again, because she trained a woman. Magali covers her ears.
Je ne veux pas l'entendre!
'I don't want to hear it!' The negative wrap again, around the verb for 'want'. And then, more quietly.
Je veux juste partir.
'I just want to leave.' The little word in the middle means 'just' or 'only'. That's all she asks. But Andréa will not be left.
Tu ne pars pas. C'est moi qui te vire!
'You're not leaving. I'm the one firing you!' The same spotlight pattern, 'it's me who'. The verb for firing someone is casual, the kind you hear in offices all the time. And she seals it.
Tu es virée!

'You're fired!' Three short words, and the last one has the feminine ending you know by now. Andréa can't stand being left, so she turns Magali's resignation into a firing. Here's the whole scene once more, a little faster.
Magali! Tu as une enveloppe?
J'en ai assez. Je pars!
Tu vas où?
Ne fais pas ça, Magali.
Je n'en peux plus, Andréa.
Je suis très fatiguée.
Bien sûr que tu es fatiguée.
On est tous fatigués. C'est l'hiver!
Prends de la gelée royale.
Fais du vélo! Ça donne des forces.
C'est comme ça que tu me remercies?
C'est moi qui t'ai formée!
Je ne veux pas l'entendre!
Je veux juste partir.
Tu ne pars pas. C'est moi qui te vire!
Tu es virée!
So Magali is gone, and Andréa has no assistant at all, which will matter very soon. If commands felt easy this time, you've already learned a lot. See you in the next scene.
Au revoir, Andréa!
